exam.answer_key_note: No official key exists. All answers were solved independently and checked against the Eritrean MoE Biology textbooks Grades 9–12 (extracted text with page markers). See confidence and review_flag on each question.

questions.stem: When molecules from the food we eat are transported through the cell membrane in a process which requires energy, what kind of transport is this?
explanation_steps: Passive transport (diffusion, osmosis) moves molecules down a concentration gradient and needs no energy from the cell.
The textbook defines active transport as transport of molecules into and out of the cell with the help of energy (ATP).
The stem says the transport requires energy, so it is active transport. Answer: C.
tips: Key word 'requires energy' (ATP) → active transport; 'no energy' → diffusion/osmosis (passive).
Osmosis is only the movement of WATER across a selectively permeable membrane.

similar_questions.stem: Root hair cells absorb mineral ions from the soil even when the ion concentration in the soil is lower than in the cell. This uptake is by:
explanation_steps: Moving ions from low to high concentration (against the gradient) needs energy.
Energy-requiring transport across a membrane is active transport. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Plant cells differ from animal cells by the presence of
explanation_steps: The textbook lists structures a plant cell has but an animal cell lacks: cell wall (cellulose), plastids such as chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole.
Endoplasmic reticulum occurs in both kinds of eukaryotic cell.
The textbook states that lysosomes (like centrioles) are found only in animal cells, so a lysosome cannot be the plant-cell feature.
Both the cell wall (C) and chloroplasts (D) are plant-only structures. Answer: E.
tips: Plant-only: cell wall, chloroplasts (plastids), large central vacuole. Animal-only (per the Grade 9 textbook): centrioles, lysosomes.
When two options are both correct, look for a combined option such as 'C and D'.

similar_questions.stem: Which pair of organelles is found in animal cells but, according to the Grade 9 textbook, not in plant cells?
explanation_steps: Cell wall, chloroplast, central vacuole and plastids are plant structures; ribosomes, mitochondria, nucleus and membrane occur in both.
The textbook describes centrioles and lysosomes as found only in animal cells. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2.2 The Cell Structure – plant cell organelles

questions.stem: One of the following is not a viral disease.
explanation_steps: The textbook lists viral diseases of humans: smallpox, common cold, chickenpox, influenza, shingles, herpes, polio, rabies, Ebola and HIV/AIDS.
Salmonellosis is caused by Salmonella bacteria (septicaemia and severe diarrhoea) – a bacterial disease.
Answer: B.
tips: Diseases whose names come from a bacterium (Salmonella → salmonellosis) are bacterial.
Bacterial diseases in the textbook: gonorrhoea, syphilis, tetanus, pneumonia, tuberculosis, salmonellosis, anthrax.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is caused by a bacterium?
explanation_steps: Polio, rabies, HIV/AIDS and chickenpox are viral diseases.
Tuberculosis is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Answer: C.

additional_textbook_refs.section: 1.4.2 Economic Importance of Bacteria – animal diseases (salmonellosis)

questions.stem: Why is the epiglottis important? Because…

options.A: it regulates the flow of chyme
options.B: it prevents food from going down into the trachea
options.C: it separates the pharynx from the nasal cavity
options.D: it is the passage through which food travels to the stomach

explanation_steps: The glottis (opening of the larynx/trachea) is guarded by a flap of tissue called the epiglottis.
During swallowing the epiglottis moves down and closes the trachea, so food passes into the oesophagus and not into the airway.
Chyme flow is regulated by the pyloric sphincter (A); the soft palate closes the nasal cavity (C); the oesophagus carries food to the stomach (D). Answer: B.
tips: Epiglottis = 'lid over the glottis'. Choking happens when food 'goes down the wrong way' past it.

similar_questions.stem: During swallowing, which structure closes off the nasal cavity so that food does not enter the nose?
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The soft palate is raised … closing the nasal cavity, and the epiglottis … closes the trachea.'
So the nasal cavity is closed by the soft palate. Answer: B.

questions.stem: An enzyme that converts sucrose to glucose and fructose is…
explanation_steps: Sucrose is a disaccharide made of glucose + fructose; its hydrolysing enzyme is sucrase.
The Grade 10 textbook names this enzyme 'sucrase' (sucrase digests sucrose to glucose and fructose). 'Invertase' is the other common name of the same enzyme (it 'inverts' cane sugar).
Lipase digests fats, nuclease nucleic acids, lactase lactose (→ glucose + galactose). Answer: D.
tips: Enzyme names usually = substrate + '-ase': sucrose → sucrase (also called invertase), maltose → maltase, lactose → lactase.

similar_questions.stem: Which enzyme breaks down lactose, and what are the products?
explanation_steps: Lactose (milk sugar) = glucose + galactose.
Its enzyme is lactase. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: the textbook calls this enzyme 'sucrase'; 'invertase' (the keyed option) does not appear in the textbook. Students must know the two names are synonyms.

questions.stem: Which of the following secondary sexual characters is NOT present in both males and females?

options.A: Hair growth in the genital area

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'In both females and males, there is a sharp increase in the growth rate and hair growth in the genital area and under the armpits.'
Deepening of the voice is listed only among the male puberty changes (with facial hair, muscle development, enlarged testes).
Answer: D.
tips: Read 'not present in both' as 'found in only one sex'.

similar_questions.stem: Which puberty change occurs in females only?

options.C: Broadening of the hips and development of breasts

explanation_steps: Pubic hair, growth spurt and armpit hair occur in both sexes; an enlarged larynx (deeper voice) is male.
Broadening of the hips and breast development are female secondary sexual characteristics. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the seminal fluid secreted by the seminal vesicles in males?

options.C: Lubricates the end of the penis during sexual intercourse
options.D: Regulates pH or neutralizes the acidity of the urethra

explanation_steps: The textbook: the seminal vesicle secretes a slightly alkaline fluid containing prostaglandins that helps regulate pH and aids movement of the sperm; semen contains food (fructose) for the sperm.
Lubricating the end of the penis is the job of the mucus-like fluid from Cowper's glands.
Answer: C.
tips: Match gland → fluid: seminal vesicle (alkaline, fructose, prostaglandins), prostate (thin milky alkaline fluid), Cowper's gland (mucus lubricant).

similar_questions.stem: Which male accessory gland secretes a mucus-like fluid that lubricates the end of the penis?
explanation_steps: The textbook assigns lubrication to the Cowper's (bulbourethral) glands. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Monoploid (haploid) gametes are produced in animals as a result of…
explanation_steps: Gametes (sperm and egg) carry one set of chromosomes (n, monoploid/haploid).
The textbook: meiosis is the special form of cell division that produces sperm and eggs; it halves the chromosome number.
Mitosis keeps the chromosome number (2n → 2n); fertilization restores 2n; 'binary fusion' is not a process that makes gametes. Answer: A.
tips: Meiosis → gametes (n). Mitosis → growth and repair (2n). Fertilization n + n → zygote 2n.

similar_questions.stem: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a human sperm cell and which division produced it?
explanation_steps: Meiosis halves the chromosome number: 46 → 23.
Sperm are produced by meiosis. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Determine the sequence of nucleotides in the mRNA transcribed from DNA having the sequence A-T-G-C-A.
explanation_steps: In transcription the mRNA is built complementary to the DNA template strand.
Base pairing DNA → RNA: A → U, T → A, G → C, C → G (RNA has uracil instead of thymine).
A-T-G-C-A → U-A-C-G-U. Answer: A.
Options B and E contain T, which never occurs in RNA; D pairs A with T and T with U, which is wrong.
tips: RNA never contains thymine (T). Eliminate any option with T at once.
Only A pairs with U; T in DNA gives A in mRNA.

similar_questions.stem: A DNA template strand reads T-A-C-G-G-A. What is the mRNA sequence?
explanation_steps: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, G→C, A→U.
mRNA: A-U-G-C-C-U. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A mitotic phase whose initial stage is marked by noticeable shortening and thickening of the chromatids (chromosomes) is…
explanation_steps: The textbook: in prophase the thread-like chromosomes appear; as prophase progresses the threads coil and become shorter and fatter, visible as two sister chromatids.
Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator; anaphase: chromatids separate to the poles; telophase: new nuclei form.
Answer: B.
tips: Order of mitosis: P-M-A-T (Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase). Condensing (shortening/thickening) is the first visible event → prophase.

similar_questions.stem: In which phase of mitosis do the sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles?
explanation_steps: Anaphase = 'apart' phase: centromeres split and chromatids are pulled to opposite poles. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Minor wording: chromosomes (made of two chromatids) shorten and thicken; the paper says 'chromatid'. Meaning is clear.

questions.stem: The change in growing insects, not only in size but a marked change in form, is…
explanation_steps: The textbook: young, growing insects change not only in size but often with a marked change in form, a phenomenon known as metamorphosis.
Hermaphroditism = one individual has both male and female organs; cephalization = concentration of sense organs in a head.
Answer: C.
tips: This stem is copied almost word for word from the textbook definition of metamorphosis.

similar_questions.stem: A butterfly passes through egg, larva, pupa and adult stages. This is called:
explanation_steps: Four stages including a pupa = complete metamorphosis (butterfly, housefly).
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Members of the class Chondrichthyes have the following characters except:
explanation_steps: The textbook: cartilaginous fishes (sharks and rays) have a mouth with a true jaw, two pairs of fins, tooth-like scales and five pairs of gill slits; fishes have a two-chambered heart.
So A, B and D are true characters of Chondrichthyes.
'Do not have jaws' is false – jawless fishes are lampreys and hagfishes, not sharks and rays. Answer: C.
tips: Chondrichthyes = cartilage skeleton (sharks, rays, skates); Osteichthyes = bony skeleton with swim bladder.

similar_questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes bony fishes (Osteichthyes) from cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes)?
explanation_steps: Both groups have jaws, gills, fins and a two-chambered heart.
Bony fishes have a bony endoskeleton and usually a swim bladder. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is pseudocoelomate?
explanation_steps: Body cavity types: acoelomate (no cavity) – flatworms; pseudocoelomate (false cavity not fully lined by mesoderm) – roundworms (nematodes); coelomate (true coelom) – annelids, arthropods, molluscs, chordates.
Cnidarians have only a gastrovascular cavity (no coelom).
Roundworms (Ascaris, hookworm) are the classic pseudocoelomates. Answer: C.
tips: Remember 'A-P-C': Acoelomate = flatworms, Pseudocoelomate = roundworms, Coelomate = annelids and higher.

similar_questions.stem: Which group of animals is acoelomate (has no body cavity)?
explanation_steps: Flatworms (Platyhelminthes) have solid bodies with no body cavity. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.note: The textbook describes nematodes but does not use the terms coelom/pseudocoelom; standard zoology applied.

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: the term 'pseudocoelomate' is not in the Grade 9 textbook (nematodes are described without body-cavity terms). Key based on standard zoology.

questions.stem: The structure of the human heart has…

options.E: Two atria and partially divided ventricles

explanation_steps: The textbook: the human heart has four chambers – two upper thin-walled atria and two lower thick-walled ventricles.
One atrium + one ventricle = fish; two atria + one ventricle = amphibian; two atria + partially divided ventricle = most reptiles.
Answer: D.
tips: Birds and mammals (including humans) have a completely four-chambered heart, which keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart.

similar_questions.stem: A frog's heart consists of:

options.E: two atria and a partly divided ventricle

explanation_steps: Amphibians have a three-chambered heart: two atria and one ventricle. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of these factors has little effect on blood flow in arteries?

options.B: total cross-sectional area of the ventricles
options.D: the amount of blood leaving the heart

explanation_steps: Blood in the arteries is driven by the pressure produced by the contracting ventricles (heart beat) and by the volume of blood pumped out of the heart; the width (cross-sectional area) of the vessels affects the resistance and speed of flow.

Contraction of skeletal muscles squeezes the thin-walled veins (and lymph vessels) and, with their valves, helps return blood to the heart; it has little effect on flow in thick-walled, high-pressure arteries.
Answer: C.
tips: Arteries = pressure from the heart. Veins and lymph vessels = skeletal-muscle pump + valves.

similar_questions.stem: Which factor mainly helps blood return to the heart through the veins of the legs?

options.A: Contraction of skeletal muscles around the veins together with valves
options.E: The semilunar valves of the aorta

explanation_steps: Veins have low pressure. Contracting leg muscles squeeze them, and their valves stop backflow. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.note: The textbook describes artery and vein structure but does not list the factors that affect arterial blood flow.

additional_textbook_refs.section: 3.1.2 Lymphatic Vessels – skeletal muscle action moves lymph

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: factors affecting arterial blood flow are not discussed in the textbook. Option B is garbled ('cross-sectional area of the ventricles' – probably 'of the arteries/vessels' was meant). Key C follows standard physiology.

questions.stem: An Rh-negative individual who has received one transfusion of Rh-positive blood should not receive a second transfusion with
explanation_steps: The textbook: when an Rh-negative person receives Rh-positive blood, the recipient's cells start producing anti-Rh antibodies; the first transfusion usually has no serious effect.
A second transfusion of Rh-positive blood would meet these anti-Rh antibodies → agglutination of the donor red cells (a serious reaction).
Rh-negative blood carries no Rh antigen, so it is safe. Answer: C.
tips: The Rh system: first exposure → sensitisation (antibodies form); second exposure → reaction. Same idea as Rh disease of the newborn in a second pregnancy.

similar_questions.stem: An Rh-negative mother carries her second Rh-positive baby after the first Rh-positive baby sensitised her. What is the risk?

options.B: Her anti-Rh antibodies may cross the placenta and destroy the baby's red cells
options.C: The baby will produce anti-A antibodies
options.D: The mother's blood becomes Rh positive

explanation_steps: After the first birth the mother formed anti-Rh antibodies.
In the second pregnancy these antibodies cross the placenta and attack the Rh-positive red cells of the fetus. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.5 Blood Types – the Rh blood group

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is true?

options.A: Hormones are made up of proteins only
options.B: Hormones are made up of proteins and minerals
options.C: Hormones are made up of vitamins only
options.D: Hormones are made up of proteins, steroids and amino acid derivatives

explanation_steps: Chemically, hormones fall into three groups: protein/peptide hormones (insulin, ADH, growth hormone), steroid hormones (oestrogen, testosterone, corticosteroids) and amino-acid derivatives (thyroxine, adrenaline).
The textbook mentions protein hormones (G10: 'some hormones are proteins') and steroid hormones of the adrenal cortex and sex glands, so 'proteins only' is wrong.
Answer: D.
tips: Examples to remember: insulin = protein; testosterone = steroid; adrenaline/thyroxine = amino-acid derivatives.

similar_questions.stem: Testosterone and oestrogen are examples of which chemical type of hormone?
explanation_steps: Sex hormones are made from cholesterol → steroids. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.note: The textbook mentions protein and steroid hormones but gives no formal chemical classification of hormones.

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: the three chemical classes of hormones are not stated explicitly in the textbook; key from standard biology (only D is scientifically acceptable).

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an incorrect statement?

options.A: Oxytocin is also known as the 'love hormone'
options.B: ADH maintains water and salt balance through the kidney
options.C: LH hormone releases the mature egg from the ovary into the oviduct
options.D: TSH stimulates the thyroid gland to produce thyroxin hormone

explanation_steps: Textbook: prolactin causes the mammary glands to develop and PRODUCE milk; oxytocin causes contraction of the uterus at childbirth and stimulates the release (let-down) of milk.
So 'prolactin causes milk releasing' is incorrect.

ADH controls water reabsorption in the kidney (water–salt balance) ✓; TSH stimulates the thyroid ✓; an LH surge triggers ovulation (release of the ovum) ✓; oxytocin is popularly called the 'love hormone' ✓ (not a textbook term).
Answer: E.
tips: Prolactin → milk Production; Oxytocin → milk Out (ejection) and uterine contraction.

similar_questions.stem: Which hormone causes contraction of the uterine muscles during childbirth?
explanation_steps: Oxytocin, released from the posterior pituitary, stimulates uterine contractions and milk ejection. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Option A uses the popular nickname 'love hormone', which is not in the textbook; option C (LH causes ovulation) is standard but the textbook only says LH acts on the corpus luteum 'after the release of an ovum'. Neither affects the key E.

questions.stem: The protein secreted by the beta cells of the pancreas is known as ______
explanation_steps: The textbook: in the islets of Langerhans, the alpha cells secrete glucagon and the beta cells secrete insulin.
Glycogen is a stored carbohydrate (not secreted); ATP is an energy molecule. Answer: A.
tips: Beta → insulin (lowers blood glucose); Alpha → glucagon (raises blood glucose).

similar_questions.stem: Which hormone raises blood glucose by stimulating the liver to break down glycogen?
explanation_steps: Glucagon from the alpha cells converts glycogen to glucose. Answer: B.

questions.stem: To find out whether a trait is homozygous or heterozygous we need a
explanation_steps: The textbook: to find out whether an organism with the dominant phenotype is homozygous (TT) or heterozygous (Tt), a test cross must be performed.
In a test cross the organism is crossed with the homozygous recessive (tt). All dominant offspring → TT; half recessive → Tt.
Answer: C.
tips: Test cross = cross with the homozygous recessive. Any recessive offspring prove the parent was heterozygous.

similar_questions.stem: A tall pea plant crossed with a dwarf plant (tt) gives 52 tall and 49 dwarf offspring. The genotype of the tall parent is:
explanation_steps: About 1 : 1 tall : dwarf in a test cross means the tall parent produced both T and t gametes.
So it is heterozygous Tt. Answer: B.

questions.stem: All are correct about saturated fats except:

options.A: They have more hydrogen atoms than unsaturated fats
options.B: They have fewer hydrogen atoms than unsaturated fats
options.D: They are solid at room temperature

explanation_steps: Fats are classified as saturated or unsaturated by the number of hydrogen atoms in their fatty acids.
Saturated fats have no C=C double bonds, so they hold the maximum number of hydrogen atoms – MORE than unsaturated fats (A is true, B is false).
The textbook: saturated fats are animal fats and are solid at room temperature (C, D true). Answer: B.
tips: 'Saturated' = saturated (full) with hydrogen. Unsaturated fats (plant oils) have C=C double bonds, fewer H atoms, and are liquid.

similar_questions.stem: Which statement about unsaturated fats is correct?

options.A: They are solid at room temperature
options.B: They are mainly animal fats such as butter and lard
options.C: They contain C=C double bonds and are liquid at room temperature
options.D: They have the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms

explanation_steps: Unsaturated fats (vegetable oils) have double bonds, fewer H atoms and are liquid. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: All are basic building blocks of a cell except:
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Biomolecules are the building blocks of cells. These include carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.'
Options B, C and D contain only these four biomolecules.
Minerals and vitamins are needed in small amounts (for regulation), but they are not the basic organic building blocks. Answer: A.
tips: The four biomolecules: Carbohydrates, Lipids, Proteins, Nucleic acids (mnemonic 'CLiP N').

similar_questions.stem: Which group of substances are the four major biomolecules of living cells?
explanation_steps: The textbook lists carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids as the biomolecules (building blocks of cells). Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: Lack of adequate protein in the diet, especially in children, causes…
explanation_steps: The textbook: protein inadequacy in the diet results in kwashiorkor (swollen belly, underweight children).
Marasmus is caused by an overall shortage of food energy (mainly carbohydrates); rickets by lack of vitamin D (and calcium); obesity by excess energy intake.
Answer: D.
tips: Kwashiorkor = protein deficiency; Marasmus = general starvation / lack of energy foods.

similar_questions.stem: A child whose diet lacks enough energy foods (carbohydrates) and total calories becomes very thin and wasted. The disease is:
explanation_steps: Severe lack of total energy (calories) → marasmus (the Grade 9 textbook links it to carbohydrate deficiency). Answer: B.

additional_textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: Odd one out:
explanation_steps: Inhalation (textbook): contraction of the diaphragm (pulls downward) and intercostal muscles (pulling the ribs outward and upward) results in the expansion of the lungs → A, B and C all belong to inhalation.
Exhalation: the diaphragm relaxes and assumes its dome shape; the chest wall moves down and in.
D is the only exhalation event. Answer: D.
tips: Inhale: diaphragm flattens (down), ribs up and out, volume ↑, pressure ↓. Exhale: diaphragm dome-shaped (up), ribs down and in.

similar_questions.stem: Which event occurs during exhalation?

options.A: Intercostal muscles contract and ribs move up
options.E: Pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure

explanation_steps: Exhalation is relaxation: the diaphragm returns to its dome shape and lung volume decreases. Answer: C.

questions.stem: ______ is a special part of the respiratory tract that functions as an airway to the lungs as well as producing sound.
explanation_steps: The textbook: the larynx (voice box) is a special part of the respiratory tract that functions as an airway to the lungs as well as producing sound; its vocal cords vibrate when air passes through them.
Answer: D.
tips: Larynx = voice box (contains vocal cords); trachea = windpipe; pharynx = throat (shared by air and food).

similar_questions.stem: The folds of elastic tissue in the larynx that vibrate to produce sound are the:
explanation_steps: Vocal cords in the larynx vibrate as air passes through them. Answer: B.

questions.stem: During seed germination, the part that first emerges through the seed coat is ______
explanation_steps: The textbook: the embryo consists of a radicle (grows into the root) and plumule (shoot); germination begins after water is absorbed and the radicle emerges first; after the radicle has emerged the epicotyl/plumule follows.
'Epigeal' is a type of germination (cotyledons above ground), not a part. Answer: B.
tips: Root first (radicle) – it anchors the seedling and absorbs water; the shoot (plumule) follows.

similar_questions.stem: In epigeal germination (e.g. bean), the cotyledons are carried above the ground by the elongation of the:
explanation_steps: In epigeal germination the hypocotyl elongates and lifts the cotyledons above the soil. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A well-known natural auxin which is produced in the apical meristem of the shoot is ______
explanation_steps: The textbook: the best-known natural auxin is indoleacetic acid (IAA), produced in the apical meristem of the shoot.
NAA is a synthetic auxin; cytokinin and ABA are different classes of plant hormones. Answer: A.
tips: Natural auxin = IAA. Synthetic auxins = NAA, 2,4-D (used as rooting powders and weed-killers).

similar_questions.stem: Which plant hormone promotes dormancy and closing of stomata during water stress?
explanation_steps: Abscisic acid (ABA) is the 'stress hormone': it causes dormancy and stomatal closure. Answer: D.

questions.stem: In the internal structure of a leaf, the upper and lower epidermis are separated by the
explanation_steps: The textbook: the upper and lower epidermis are separated by the mesophyll, which consists of a palisade layer and a spongy layer.
Palisade and spongy layers are only parts of the mesophyll; the cuticle is the waxy layer outside the epidermis.
Answer: C.
tips: Mesophyll = 'middle leaf' = palisade + spongy layers together.

similar_questions.stem: Which layer of the leaf contains the most chloroplasts and is the main site of photosynthesis?
explanation_steps: Palisade cells are tightly packed, column-shaped and rich in chloroplasts. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The process by which the second male nucleus unites with the two polar nuclei to form an endosperm is called ______
explanation_steps: In flowering plants the pollen tube delivers two male nuclei: one fuses with the egg (→ zygote), the other fuses with the two polar nuclei (→ endosperm).
The textbook: '…the two polar nuclei, forming an endosperm. This process is called double fertilization, and is only found in flowering plants.'
A zygote and the micropyle are structures, not processes. Answer: B.
tips: The fusion of the second male nucleus with the two polar nuclei is also called 'triple fusion'; together with egg fertilization it makes 'double fertilization'.

similar_questions.stem: In double fertilization, the fusion of one male nucleus with the egg cell forms the:
explanation_steps: Male nucleus + egg → zygote (2n), which grows into the embryo. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Strictly, male nucleus + two polar nuclei is 'triple fusion', one half of double fertilization; the paper follows the textbook wording, which calls it double fertilization.

questions.stem: Identify the incorrect statement about evolution.

options.A: evolution refers to a gradual change over time through which new species arise from existing ones
options.B: studies on geographic distribution and anatomy of organisms are helpful to support the theory of evolution
options.C: evolution has resulted in the diversity of life forms we see today
options.D: changes considered in evolution refer to changes within an individual

explanation_steps: The textbook defines evolution as gradual change in earlier, simpler forms of life over time, producing present-day organisms (A, C true).
Evidence for evolution includes comparative anatomy and geographical distribution (B true).
Evolution acts on populations over many generations; changes within one individual's lifetime (growth, acquired traits) are not evolution → D is incorrect.
E ('B and D') is wrong because B is true. Answer: D.
tips: Individuals develop; POPULATIONS evolve.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT evidence for evolution?
explanation_steps: Fossils, homologous organs, embryology and biochemistry are textbook evidences for evolution.
Muscles built by exercise are acquired characters and are not inherited. Answer: D.

questions.stem: Greater similarity between two organisms reveals that they have
explanation_steps: Comparative anatomy (homologous organs) and biochemistry show that the more features two organisms share, the more recently they shared a common ancestor.
The textbook: homologous organs have the same structure, inherited from a common ancestor. Answer: B.
tips: Homologous structures (same basic plan, different function) → common ancestry. Analogous structures (same function, different plan) → no close relationship.

similar_questions.stem: The forelimb of a human, the wing of a bat and the flipper of a whale have the same basic bone pattern. They are called ___ organs and suggest ___.
explanation_steps: Same structural plan with different functions = homologous organs, evidence of a common ancestor. Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are adaptations of animals to cold temperature, except:

options.B: dry waterproof skin, especially in reptiles

explanation_steps: Textbook adaptations to low temperature: hormonal changes that boost the metabolic rate, good appetite, shivering, insulation by fur/feathers and fat, hibernation, basking, small body projections.
So fat layer (A), high metabolism (C) and fur (D) are cold adaptations.
Dry, waterproof (scaly) skin in reptiles is an adaptation to dry conditions – it reduces water loss, not heat loss. Answer: B.
tips: Cold: insulate (fur, feathers, fat) + make more heat (metabolism, shivering) + reduce surface (small ears). Heat/dry: large ears, no fat layer, sweating, waterproof skin.

similar_questions.stem: The camel has no thick layer of fat under its skin and has long thin legs. This is an adaptation to:
explanation_steps: The textbook lists 'absence of fat layer' (camel) among adaptations to high temperature. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment
textbook_ref.section: 4.3.1 Adaptations of Animals to Low Temperatures

questions.stem: Which of the following plants is highly adapted to a saline environment?
explanation_steps: The textbook (adaptations of plants to salt): mangroves cover a great part of seashores and grow in salty, oxygen-poor mud (with breathing roots).
Cactus is adapted to dry (xerophytic) conditions; grass and corn are not salt-tolerant. Answer: C.
tips: Salt → mangrove (halophyte). Drought → cactus (xerophyte). Water → water lily (hydrophyte).

similar_questions.stem: A plant with thick fleshy stems, spines instead of leaves and a thick waxy cuticle is adapted to:
explanation_steps: Spines and fleshy water-storing stems (cactus) reduce water loss → dry (desert) adaptation. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment

questions.stem: The main ways in which kidney failure is treated are by
explanation_steps: The textbook: the two main ways kidney failure is treated are an artificial kidney (dialysis machine – short-term) or a kidney transplant (long-term).
Drinking plenty of water does not replace kidney function. Answer: E.
tips: Dialysis = artificial kidney, a short-term solution; transplant = long-term solution.

similar_questions.stem: A dialysis machine removes urea from a patient's blood. This machine is also known as:
explanation_steps: The textbook calls the dialysis machine an artificial kidney. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Internal receptors detect stimuli related to the following, except
explanation_steps: The textbook: internal receptors detect stimuli related to muscle length and tension, limb position, pain, blood composition, blood volume, blood pressure, body temperature, etc.
Light is an external stimulus detected by the photoreceptors of the eye (an external receptor). Answer: D.
tips: Internal receptors monitor conditions INSIDE the body; the eye, ear, nose, tongue and skin receive external stimuli.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an external receptor?
explanation_steps: The eye's photoreceptors receive light from outside the body. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following organs serves as an organ of excretion, temperature regulation and defence against infection?
explanation_steps: Excretion: the skin excretes sweat (excess water, salts and urea) through sweat glands.
Temperature regulation: sweating, vasodilation/vasoconstriction and hair in the skin control heat loss.
Defence: the intact skin is the first physical barrier against microorganisms.
Lungs, liver and kidney are excretory organs but not all three functions. Answer: B.
tips: The skin is the only organ that combines excretion (sweat), thermoregulation and a physical barrier against pathogens.

similar_questions.stem: Which excretory organ removes carbon dioxide and water vapour from the body?
explanation_steps: The lungs expel CO₂ and water by exhalation. Answer: C.

additional_textbook_refs.section: 5.4 The Control of Body Temperature – skin
4 The Immune System – skin as barrier

questions.stem: Which one of the following is not a function of the hypothalamus?

options.A: control of body temperature and blood pressure
options.B: regulation of the pituitary gland's secretion of hormones

explanation_steps: The textbook: the hypothalamus contains centres controlling body temperature, blood pressure, water balance, appetite, sleep and some emotions; it regulates the pituitary gland's secretion; sensations such as pleasure and feeling 'good' after a meal are related to it.
Voluntary muscular movement is controlled by the cerebrum (frontal lobe motor area), with the cerebellum coordinating it.
Answer: D.
tips: Cerebrum = voluntary actions and thinking; cerebellum = balance and coordination; medulla = heartbeat and breathing reflexes; hypothalamus = homeostasis and pituitary control.

similar_questions.stem: Which part of the brain controls breathing rate and heartbeat?
explanation_steps: The textbook: the medulla contains the respiratory centre and the heartbeat centre. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Repeated abortion (miscarriage) happens after fertilization in a woman. This is due to an abnormality of
explanation_steps: After ovulation the corpus luteum secretes progesterone; later the placenta takes over.
The textbook: if the egg is fertilized, progesterone keeps the lining of the uterus from disintegrating; without it the lining breaks down (as in menstruation).
A shortage of progesterone therefore causes the embryo to be lost. Answer: C.
tips: Progesterone = 'pro-gestation' hormone: it maintains pregnancy.

similar_questions.stem: Which hormone stimulates the development of follicles in the ovary?
explanation_steps: FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) promotes development of the follicle. Answer: A.

questions.review_flag: Wording in the original ('Continuously abortion happens…') is ungrammatical; interpreted as repeated miscarriage.

questions.stem: A reflex action:

options.B: doesn't require the central nervous system

explanation_steps: The textbook: simple reflex behaviour is an inherited, unvarying, automatic response to a particular stimulus; reflex arcs mediate rapid, automatic or involuntary behaviour.

The reflex arc passes through the spinal cord (part of the CNS), so B is false; reflexes protect the body (withdrawing a hand from a hot object) so C is false; all vertebrates show reflexes, so D is false.
Answer: A.
tips: Reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → associative (relay) neuron in the spinal cord → motor neuron → effector.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a simple reflex?

options.B: Blinking when an object comes close to the eye

explanation_steps: Blinking is automatic and involuntary; the others are learned voluntary actions. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Original option C reads 'has no protective valve' – typo for 'value'. Does not affect the key.

questions.stem: In which terrestrial biome do you usually observe high diversity of species?
explanation_steps: The textbook: tropical rain forests are in the equatorial belt; warm, wet climate all year; this biome harbours more plant and animal species than any other terrestrial environment.
Tundra and taiga are cold with few species; grasslands have moderate diversity. Answer: C.
tips: Diversity rises with warmth and rainfall: rain forest > grassland > taiga > tundra/desert.

similar_questions.stem: Which biome is treeless, cold, and has permanently frozen subsoil (permafrost)?
explanation_steps: Tundra: very cold, short growing season, permafrost, no trees. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.5 Biomes of the World – tropical rain forest

questions.stem: Identify the dental formula of a carnivorous animal from the following (upper/lower teeth on one side):
explanation_steps: Carnivores (e.g. dog) have all four types of teeth, including large pointed canines for seizing and tearing flesh.
D: i 3/3, c 1/1, pm 4/4, m 2/3 → per side 3+1+4+2 = 10 upper and 3+1+4+3 = 11 lower = 21; ×2 = 42 teeth (the dog's formula).

A (5 + 10 = 15 per side → 30 teeth; no upper incisors, no canines – sheep-like) and C (no upper incisors or upper canines) are herbivore formulas; B (2 upper incisors, no canines, a gap/diastema) is a rabbit-type herbivore.
Answer: D.
tips: Canines present in both jaws (c 1/1) → carnivore or omnivore. No canines and a gap (diastema) → herbivore.
Total teeth = (sum of upper + lower numbers) × 2.

similar_questions.stem: How many teeth does an animal with the dental formula i 2/2, c 1/1, pm 2/2, m 3/3 have, and which animal is it?
explanation_steps: This is the adult human formula given in the textbook. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2.3 The Mouth – teeth and dental formula (Activity 1.12)

questions.review_flag: Option C is garbled in the original ('c 0/1m pm 3/2'); read as c 0/1, pm 3/2. The options are the four formulas of textbook Activity 1.12 (G10 p.32).

questions.stem: ______ is a smooth, double-layered tissue which covers the bone.
explanation_steps: The textbook: bones are made up of three tissue layers – periosteum, compact bone and spongy bone. 'The periosteum is a smooth, double-layered tissue, which covers the bone.'
Answer: B.
tips: Outside → inside: periosteum → compact bone → spongy bone → marrow cavity.

similar_questions.stem: Which part of a long bone contains red bone marrow that produces blood cells?
explanation_steps: Red marrow fills the spaces of spongy bone (especially at the ends of long bones). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not part of the axial skeleton?
explanation_steps: The textbook: the axial skeleton consists of the skull, vertebral column and thorax (sternum and ribs).
The appendicular skeleton consists of the limbs and the girdles (pectoral and pelvic) that attach them.
Answer: D.
tips: Axial = along the body axis (skull, backbone, ribs, sternum). Appendicular = appendages + girdles.

similar_questions.stem: The bone to which the legs are attached is part of the:
explanation_steps: The legs attach to the pelvic (hip) girdle, which belongs to the appendicular skeleton. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A female would be colour blind only if:

options.A: Only the father is colour blind
options.B: The mother is a carrier and the father is colour blind
options.C: Only the mother is colour blind
options.D: The mother is a carrier and the father is normal

explanation_steps: Colour blindness is X-linked recessive (Xᶜ). A girl receives one X from each parent and must be XᶜXᶜ to be colour blind.
The textbook: 'For females to be affected by sex-linked characters, both of the parents must have recessive alleles.'
B: mother XᶜX (carrier) × father XᶜY → daughters XᶜXᶜ (colour blind) or XᶜX → a colour-blind daughter is possible.
A: father XᶜY × normal mother XX → daughters XᶜX carriers only. C: colour-blind mother × NORMAL father → daughters XᶜX carriers only. D: carrier × normal father → daughters normal or carriers.
Answer: B.
tips: A daughter always gets her father's X. If the father has normal vision, no daughter can be colour blind.

similar_questions.stem: A colour-blind man marries a woman who is homozygous normal. What proportion of their sons will be colour blind?
explanation_steps: Sons receive their X from the mother (normal X) and Y from the father.
So no son is colour blind (daughters are all carriers). Answer: A.

questions.stem: What was Mendel's purpose in choosing the garden pea plant?

options.A: because they have a short germination time
options.B: because their pollination system can be easily monitored and controlled
options.C: because peas produce few seeds after crossing over
options.D: because they have clear contrasting characters

explanation_steps: Textbook reasons: peas grow quickly and mature in one season; pollination is easy and can be controlled artificially (self or cross); they produce fertile seeds after crossing; they have contrasting characters (tall/short, round/wrinkled…).
A (short life cycle – worded as 'germination time'), B and D match; C is false (peas produce many fertile seeds; 'crossing over' is a meiosis term).
Answer: E.
tips: Mendel's pea advantages: short life cycle, controllable pollination, many fertile seeds, clear contrasting traits.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a reason why Mendel chose the garden pea?

options.C: They can be self- or cross-pollinated
options.D: They produce sterile seeds after crossing

explanation_steps: The textbook says peas produce FERTILE seeds after crossing. Answer: D.

questions.review_flag: Option A says 'short germination time'; the textbook reason is that peas 'grow quickly and mature in one season' (short life cycle). Key E assumes the setter meant this.

questions.stem: Which one is incorrect about the unborn baby during pregnancy?

options.A: Food and oxygen pass from the mother to the fetus through the umbilical artery
options.B: Waste materials and CO₂ pass away from the fetus through the umbilical artery
options.D: The placenta is the structure that connects the fetus to its mother

explanation_steps: The textbook: the umbilical cord has arteries and veins; the VEIN transports food and oxygenated blood from the placenta to the embryo, while the ARTERY carries waste and deoxygenated blood from the embryo to the placenta.
So A is incorrect (it should be the umbilical vein); B is correct.
The fetus gets oxygen through the placenta, so its lungs do not function until birth (C correct); the placenta links the fetus (via the cord) with the mother's uterus (D acceptable).
Answer: A.
tips: Umbilical vein → TO the fetus (oxygenated). Umbilical arteries → AWAY from the fetus (deoxygenated) – just like 'arteries carry blood away from the heart'.

similar_questions.stem: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus?
explanation_steps: The textbook: the vein of the umbilical cord transports food and oxygenated blood from the placenta to the embryo. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is incorrect about the lymphatic system?

options.A: It is used to keep the fluid balance in the interstitial spaces
options.C: Lymph consists of water, waste materials, cell products and digested fats
options.D: There is no pumping organ in the lymphatic system

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The lymphatic system is a one-way circulation system, from the interstitial spaces to the blood circulation … lymph travels in only one direction: from the body organs to the heart.' The blood circulatory system is two-way.
Lymph is moved by skeletal muscle contraction, breathing movements and smooth muscle – there is no heart-like pump (D true); it returns tissue fluid (A true).
Answer: B.
tips: Circulatory system: two-way, pumped by the heart. Lymphatic system: one-way (tissues → veins), no pump, valves prevent backflow.

similar_questions.stem: What moves lymph through the lymphatic vessels?

options.B: Contraction of skeletal muscles and breathing movements

explanation_steps: The textbook names contraction of skeletal muscles, action of the breathing muscles and smooth muscle in the vessel walls. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.2 Comparison between the Lymphatic System and the Circulatory System

questions.stem: Lymph nodes are bean-shaped organs containing a large number of ______
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Lymph nodes are bean-shaped organs containing large numbers of leukocytes.'
Leukocytes (white blood cells, mainly lymphocytes and macrophages) filter and destroy microorganisms in the lymph.
Erythrocytes = red corpuscles (A and D are the same thing); thrombocytes = platelets. Answer: C.
tips: Swollen lymph nodes ('glands') during an infection = many white blood cells at work.

similar_questions.stem: Which cells in lymph nodes engulf and destroy microorganisms filtered from the lymph?
explanation_steps: Macrophages (a type of white blood cell) engulf pathogens. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Two individuals are relatives if they:

options.A: have widow's peak and continuous hair line

explanation_steps: Relatives share inherited traits; the textbook lists inherited human traits including free/attached ear lobes, tongue rolling, widow's peak, fingerprints and skin colour.

Same blood type (B) is shared by millions of unrelated people; behaviour (C) is largely learned; A is self-contradictory (widow's peak and a continuous hairline are alternative forms of the same trait).
Fingerprint patterns are inherited and very individual; similarity of fingerprints (and, in modern practice, DNA fingerprints) is the best indicator of relatedness among the options.
Answer: D (setter's most likely intention).
tips: No single visible trait PROVES relationship; DNA fingerprinting is used in paternity testing.

similar_questions.stem: Which method is used today to establish whether a man is the biological father of a child?
explanation_steps: DNA fingerprinting compares inherited DNA patterns; a child's pattern comes half from each parent. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.note: Textbook lists inherited traits but does not discuss how to establish relatedness.

questions.review_flag: Poorly constructed item: no option can prove that two people are relatives; option A is self-contradictory (widow's peak vs continuous hairline are contrasting traits). Key D (fingerprints) is the most defensible; the setter may have intended E. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: One of the following is not true about sex-linked characters.

options.A: Males with sex-linked disorders are more numerous than females
options.B: Males inherit them from their mother only
options.C: They are determined by genes located on the X chromosome only
options.D: Men are more vulnerable to sex-linked disorders

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Sex-linked characters are those characters which are due to genes located on sex chromosomes. Most sex-linked genes are carried on the X chromosome. The Y chromosome carries few genes.'
So 'on the X chromosome ONLY' (C) contradicts the textbook definition.

A and D are true (the textbook: they usually affect males). B is true for X-linked traits (a son's X comes from his mother) but would be false for the few Y-linked genes, which pass from father to son.
Answer: C (B is also defensible if Y-linked genes are considered, so both are accepted).
tips: Sex-linked = on a sex chromosome (X or Y). X-linked recessive disorders: colour blindness, haemophilia – more common in males.

similar_questions.stem: Haemophilia is caused by an X-linked recessive allele. A normal man marries a carrier woman. What is the chance that a son will have haemophilia?
explanation_steps: Mother XᴴXʰ, father XᴴY. Sons receive Xᴴ or Xʰ from the mother with equal chance.
So 1/2 (50%) of sons are haemophiliac. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Two defensible answers: C contradicts the textbook definition (genes on sex chromosomes, mostly X); B is false for Y-linked genes. Both accepted.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a cause of deafness in humans?

options.C: pointed objects entering the auditory canal

explanation_steps: The textbook: frequent causes of deafness are a calcified or pierced eardrum; excessive noise, strong blows on the cheek, pointed objects entering the auditory canal and attack from insects also affect the structures that aid in hearing.
All four options are listed. Answer: E.
tips: This list is taken directly from the textbook paragraph 'Defects in hearing'.

similar_questions.stem: Deafness caused by fusion of the ear ossicles results because:

options.B: vibrations cannot be transmitted from the eardrum to the inner ear
options.E: the cochlea produces too much fluid

explanation_steps: The ossicles (hammer, anvil, stirrup) transmit vibrations to the oval window; if fused they cannot vibrate. Answer: B.

questions.stem: When is sound formed in the larynx, as air passes through it?
explanation_steps: Sound is produced when air passes the vocal cords and makes them vibrate (textbook).
We speak with air being pushed OUT of the lungs, i.e. during exhalation.
Cellular and anaerobic respiration are chemical processes in cells, not air movement. Answer: B.
tips: Try speaking while breathing in – it is very difficult; speech uses exhaled air.

similar_questions.stem: Which structure vibrates to produce the voice when exhaled air passes over it?
explanation_steps: The vocal cords of the larynx vibrate as air passes through them. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.note: The textbook says vocal cords vibrate when air passes; that this happens during exhalation is general knowledge.

questions.stem: Smooth muscles are located in the walls of the following, except:
explanation_steps: The textbook: smooth muscles are located in the walls of the hollow organs, blood vessels, eyes, glands and skin; the walls of the stomach, intestines, urinary bladder and uterus are formed by smooth muscle.
The heart wall is made of cardiac muscle, a separate type of involuntary muscle. Answer: D.
tips: Three muscle types: skeletal (voluntary, striated), smooth (involuntary, non-striated, hollow organs), cardiac (involuntary, striated, heart only).

similar_questions.stem: Which type of muscle is striated but involuntary?
explanation_steps: Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle but contracts involuntarily. Answer: C.

questions.stem: In the life cycle of insects there are two types of metamorphosis, complete and incomplete. The correct order of development in incomplete metamorphosis is
explanation_steps: The textbook: insects like grasshoppers undergo incomplete metamorphosis with only three stages – egg, nymphs (immature stages) and adult (imago).
The nymph moults several times (several nymph stages) before becoming the adult, so 'egg → nymph → nymph → imago' shows this order.
D (egg → larva → pupa → imago) is complete metamorphosis (butterfly, housefly). Answer: C.
tips: Incomplete: no pupa (egg → nymph → adult). Complete: with pupa (egg → larva → pupa → adult).

similar_questions.stem: Which insect undergoes complete metamorphosis?
explanation_steps: The textbook gives the butterfly and housefly as examples of complete metamorphosis. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Arrows are drawn as dashes in the original ('Egg-----nymph------nymph------imago'); converted to →.

questions.stem: An injection given to a person who is bitten by a snake helps to develop
explanation_steps: Snake anti-venom is a serum containing ready-made antibodies produced in another animal (e.g. a horse).

The textbook: artificial acquired passive immunity is acquired when an individual receives antibodies produced in another individual or animal; it gives immediate but short-term protection – useful when there is no time for the body to make its own antibodies.
Answer: D.
tips: Active = your own body makes antibodies (after infection = natural; after vaccine = artificial). Passive = ready-made antibodies given (mother → baby = natural; serum injection = artificial).

similar_questions.stem: A baby receives antibodies from its mother's first breast milk (colostrum). This is:
explanation_steps: Ready-made antibodies received naturally from the mother → natural passive immunity. Answer: C.

questions.section: Part II – Fill in the blank space
questions.stem: Fill in the blank: The 'lub' sound is caused by the vibration of the heart when the ______ valves close. (1 pt)
questions.answer: Atrioventricular (AV) valves – the tricuspid and bicuspid (mitral) valves.
explanation_steps: The heart makes two sounds per beat: 'lub' (first, longer) and 'dub' (second, shorter).
At the start of ventricular systole the ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure and the atrioventricular valves close (textbook G10 p.53) – their closure produces 'lub'.
'Dub' is produced a moment later when the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves close at the start of diastole.
marking_points: Atrioventricular valves (or tricuspid and bicuspid/mitral valves) close (1)
tips: Lub = AV valves close (start of ventricular contraction). Dub = semilunar valves close (end of contraction).
'Tricuspid and bicuspid' or 'mitral' earns the mark; 'semilunar' does not.

similar_questions.stem: Fill in the blank: The second heart sound, 'dub', is produced when the ______ valves close.
explanation_steps: After ventricular contraction the ventricular pressure falls; blood tends to flow back from the aorta and pulmonary artery and pushes the semilunar valves shut → 'dub'.

textbook_ref.section: 2.1.1 The Human Heart – heart valves and cardiac cycle
textbook_ref.note: The textbook explains AV-valve closure in the cardiac cycle but does not mention the 'lub-dub' heart sounds.

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: heart sounds ('lub'/'dub') are not described in the textbook; answer from standard physiology.

questions.section: Part II – Fill in the blank space
questions.stem: Fill in the blank: The minimum amount of stimulus needed to begin transmitting an impulse is known as ______. (1 pt)
explanation_steps: The textbook: the minimum stimulus strength that makes a neuron respond is known as the neuron's threshold.
A stimulus below the threshold does not generate an impulse; a stimulus above the threshold produces a full impulse (all-or-none response).
tips: All-or-none law: once the threshold is reached, the impulse size does not increase with stronger stimuli.

similar_questions.stem: Fill in the blank: A neuron responds completely or not at all to a stimulus; this is called the ______ response.
explanation_steps: Below threshold → no impulse; at or above threshold → a full-size impulse. Hence 'all-or-none'.

questions.section: Part II – Fill in the blank space
questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Treponema pallidum are types of harmful bacteria and cause the diseases called ______ and ______ respectively. (1 pt)
explanation_steps: The textbook: gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted disease caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Syphilis is another STD caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum.
Order matters ('respectively'): first gonorrhoea, then syphilis.
tips: Both are bacterial STDs and can be treated with antibiotics; HIV/AIDS, herpes and genital warts are viral STDs.

similar_questions.stem: Fill in the blank: The bacterium Clostridium tetani causes ______, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes ______.
explanation_steps: Both diseases appear in the textbook list of human diseases caused by bacteria (gonorrhoea, syphilis, tetanus, pneumonia, tuberculosis).

textbook_ref.section: 1.4.2 The Economic Importance of Bacteria – human diseases

questions.review_flag: Spelling in the original: 'Neisseria gonorrhea and tripanema pallidum' – correct names are Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Treponema pallidum (corrected in the stem).

questions.section: Part II – Fill in the blank space
questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Some bacteria such as E. coli transfer their genetic material from one organism to another through a primitive means of sexual reproduction known as ______. (1 pt)
explanation_steps: The textbook (Kingdom Monera): some bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, transfer their genetic material from one organism to another through a primitive means of sexual reproduction called conjugation.
In conjugation two cells join by a bridge (pilus) and DNA passes from one to the other; bacteria otherwise reproduce asexually by binary fission.
tips: Conjugation also occurs in Paramecium and Spirogyra (textbook), but in bacteria it is the 'primitive sexual reproduction'.

similar_questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Under favourable conditions bacteria reproduce asexually by a simple division of one cell into two, called ______.
explanation_steps: One bacterial cell copies its DNA and splits into two identical daughter cells – binary fission.

questions.stem: Which one of the six nutrients might a person need to restrict after surgical removal of the gall bladder? Give a reason. (1 pt)
questions.answer: Fats (lipids). Bile, made by the liver, is normally stored and concentrated in the gall bladder and released in large amounts when fatty food enters the duodenum. Bile salts emulsify fats into tiny droplets so that lipase can digest them. Without a gall bladder, only a small, continuous trickle of bile reaches the intestine, so a large fatty meal cannot be emulsified and digested properly (causing indigestion/diarrhoea). The person should therefore restrict fatty foods.
explanation_steps: Six nutrients: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids (fats), vitamins, minerals, water.
The textbook: bile is stored in the gall bladder; bile salts break fats into very tiny droplets (emulsification) to increase their surface area for digestion.
Removing the gall bladder removes the bile store, so fat digestion is limited → restrict fats.
marking_points: Reason: bile (stored in gall bladder) is needed to emulsify fats; without the store, fat digestion is poor (0.5)
tips: State the nutrient AND the reason (bile storage/emulsification) – half a mark each.
Bile contains no enzymes; it works physically (emulsification) and neutralises acidic chyme.

similar_questions.stem: Why is bile called a digestive juice although it contains no enzymes?
similar_questions.answer: Because bile salts emulsify fats – they break large fat droplets into tiny droplets, increasing the surface area on which lipase acts – and bile neutralises the acidic chyme, giving the alkaline conditions intestinal enzymes need.
explanation_steps: The textbook: bile is essential for the digestion of lipids although it contains no enzymes.
Emulsification is a physical change that speeds up chemical digestion by lipase.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2.6 The Small Intestine – liver and bile

questions.stem: Write at least two differences between a food chain and a food web. (2 pts)
questions.answer:
1. A food chain is a single, linear sequence of feeding (energy flow) from a producer through one consumer at each level; a food web is a network of many interconnected food chains.
2. In a food chain each organism eats only one type of food and is eaten by one type of consumer; in a food web an animal may have several food sources and several predators.
3. A food chain is simple and short; a food web is complex.
4. A food web is more stable: if one food source is removed, consumers can switch to others; in a single food chain, removing one link affects all the organisms after it.
explanation_steps: Food chain (textbook): the linear sequence of energy flow in the form of food from a producer to consumers.
Food web (textbook): composed of several interconnecting food chains; a predator does not live exclusively on one type of food.
Write the differences as contrasting pairs (chain … whereas web …).
marking_points: Any two correct contrasting differences, 1 pt each: linear/single pathway vs interconnected network; one food source vs several food sources; simple vs complex; less stable vs more stable
tips: Give the differences as clear pairs, e.g. 'linear vs. network', 'one food source vs. many', 'less stable vs. more stable'.

similar_questions.stem: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk. (a) Name the producer and the secondary consumer. (b) What happens to the frog population if the snakes are removed?
similar_questions.answer: (a) Producer: grass; secondary consumer: frog. (b) With fewer predators the frog population first increases (then may fall later as grasshoppers, their food, are over-eaten).
explanation_steps: Producer = green plant; primary consumer eats the plant (grasshopper); secondary consumer eats the primary consumer (frog).
Removing a predator releases its prey from predation.

textbook_ref.section: 3.3 Food Relationships – food chains and food webs

questions.stem: Mention the four lobes of the cerebral hemisphere. (2 pts)
questions.answer: Frontal lobe, parietal lobe, temporal lobe and occipital lobe.
explanation_steps: The textbook: each cerebral hemisphere is divided into lobes named after the skull bones overlying them.
Frontal – voluntary motor functions, motivation, smell, mood; parietal – reception and evaluation of sensory information; temporal – hearing, smell, memory; occipital – vision.
tips: Mnemonic 'F-P-T-O' (front → top → side → back): Frontal, Parietal, Temporal, Occipital.

similar_questions.stem: Which lobe of the cerebrum receives and interprets visual input, and which receives input for hearing?
similar_questions.answer: Occipital lobe – vision; temporal lobe – hearing (and smell, memory).
explanation_steps: The textbook: the occipital lobe functions in reception and integration of visual input; the temporal lobe receives and evaluates input for smell and hearing.

textbook_ref.section: 8.2.1 The Central Nervous System – the cerebrum

questions.stem: Half of the offspring have free ear lobes and half have attached ear lobes. Using a Punnett square, find the genotypes of their parents if free ear lobe is dominant over attached ear lobe. (2 pts)
questions.answer:
Let F = free ear lobe (dominant), f = attached ear lobe (recessive). A 1 : 1 ratio comes from a cross of a heterozygous parent with a homozygous recessive parent: Ff (free) × ff (attached).
Punnett square: gametes of Ff = F, f; gametes of ff = f, f →
      |  F  |  f
  f   | Ff  | ff
  f   | Ff  | ff
Offspring: 2 Ff (free) : 2 ff (attached) = 1 : 1 (50% free, 50% attached). Parents' genotypes: Ff and ff.
explanation_steps: Attached-lobed offspring (ff) must receive an f allele from EACH parent, so both parents carry f.
If both parents were Ff the ratio would be 3 free : 1 attached; if one parent were FF all offspring would be free.
Only Ff × ff gives 1 free : 1 attached – this is a test-cross ratio.
Draw the Punnett square to show 2 Ff : 2 ff.
tips: A 1 : 1 phenotype ratio in a monohybrid cross always means heterozygous × homozygous recessive.
3 : 1 → both heterozygous; all dominant → at least one parent homozygous dominant.

similar_questions.stem: In humans, tongue rolling (R) is dominant over non-rolling (r). Two tongue-rollers have a non-rolling child. What are the parents' genotypes and the chance that their next child is a roller?
similar_questions.answer: Both parents are Rr. Rr × Rr → 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr, so the chance of a roller is 3/4 (75%).
explanation_steps: The non-roller child is rr and received r from each parent, so both rolling parents are heterozygous (Rr).
Punnett square Rr × Rr gives 3 rollers : 1 non-roller.

questions.stem:
Label the parts of Euglena (A–H) shown in the diagram. (4 pts)
Diagram (described): a spindle-shaped single cell. A = the long whip-like thread at the front end; B = bracket over the flask-shaped opening/depression at the front end; C = the dark body beside the reservoir near the front; D = a small round clear vacuole near the reservoir; E = the long rod-shaped bodies scattered in the cytoplasm; F = the large round body in the lower half; G = the small dark body inside F; H = the thin outer covering of the cell.
questions.image_alt: Line drawing of Euglena with labels A–H: A flagellum, B anterior reservoir/gullet region, C dark eyespot, D small vacuole, E rod-shaped chloroplasts, F nucleus, G dark body inside the nucleus, H outer covering.
questions.answer: A – flagellum; B – reservoir (with gullet/cytopharynx); C – eyespot (stigma); D – contractile vacuole; E – chloroplast; F – nucleus; G – nucleolus (endosome); H – pellicle.
explanation_steps: The textbook (Euglena, Fig. 2.9): whip-like flagellum at the anterior end, attached at the base of the flask-shaped reservoir; a contractile vacuole near the reservoir; funnel-like mouth leading to a short gullet; numerous chloroplasts; a light-sensitive eyespot (stigma) near the anterior end; no cell wall but a flexible pellicle; a nucleus.

Match: the long thread (A) is the flagellum; the anterior depression (B) is the reservoir/gullet; the dark pigment spot beside it (C) is the eyespot; the small clear vacuole (D) is the contractile vacuole.
The many rod-shaped bodies (E) are chloroplasts; the large round body (F) is the nucleus, and the dark body within it (G) the nucleolus (endosome); the outer covering (H) is the pellicle.
tips: Eight labels × 0.5 pt. Accept 'gullet/cytopharynx' for B and 'stigma' for C.
Euglena is both plant-like (chloroplasts) and animal-like (no cell wall, moves by flagellum).

similar_questions.stem: State the function of each: (a) flagellum, (b) eyespot, (c) contractile vacuole, (d) pellicle of Euglena.
similar_questions.answer: (a) Locomotion – pulls the cell through water. (b) Detects light so the cell swims towards favourable light for photosynthesis. (c) Collects excess water and expels it (osmoregulation). (d) Thin flexible covering that maintains the body shape (Euglena has no cell wall).
explanation_steps: All four functions are stated or implied in the textbook description of Euglena (G9 pp.71–72).
